title: Effect of a workplace-based visuo-motor head-tracking training with and without balance exercises on pain, function, and cervical sensorimotor control in office workers with chronic non-specific neck pain: a four-arm randomized controlled trial
summary:
Neck pain is among the most common musculoskeletal complaints worldwide and substantially impairs quality of life as well as work ability. It is frequently associated with absenteeism in the workplace (Guerra-Arencibia et al., 2024; Kazeminasab et al., 2022; Kose et al., 2007). Office workers are particularly affected, as they spend long periods sitting each day, adopt monotonous postures, and often maintain a forward head position (Dandale et al., 2023; Paksaichol et al., 2012; Szeto et al., 2002). In this occupational group, the annual prevalence of neck pain is reported to be as high as 69% (Hoy et al., 2010; Sihawong et al., 2011). In addition to physical risk factors such as unfavorable postures, psychosocial factors also play an important role. Depressive mood states and perceived muscle tension have been repeatedly described in this context (Kim et al., 2018). Typical findings include pronounced muscle tension as well as increased pressure pain sensitivity in the neck and shoulder region (Abdullah Nasser Alshahrani et al., 2024). Furthermore, individuals with chronic neck pain frequently experience sleep disturbances, which further exacerbate pain symptoms (Artner et al., 2012). Studies show that sleep disturbances are significantly associated with neck pain, with the strength of this association increasing with longer duration of sleep problems (Yabe et al., 2022). In addition, sleep deprivation leads to increased pain sensitivity and intensifies subjective pain perception (Chang et al., 2022).
A central role in non-specific neck pain is attributed to impaired sensorimotor control. Proprioception as well as movement and postural control of the cervical spine are often restricted in affected individuals (Preiss, Taube, et al., 2024; Qu et al., 2022). During office work, additional postural changes occur that are associated with impaired proprioceptive feedback and may further increase the risk of persistent complaints. Current research indicates that targeted training can have a positive effect on sensorimotor function as well as pain perception in individuals with neck pain. For example, a study by Beinert and Taube (2013) demonstrated that a five-week balance training program in individuals with a history of subclinical neck pain led to a significant improvement in sensorimotor function, measured by the accuracy of head repositioning. At the same time, a reduction in neck pain was observed. However, the association between cervical sensorimotor function and the intensity of neck pain was found to be rather weak. In addition to longer-term training interventions, immediate effects have also been demonstrated. A single visuo-motor tracking task resulted in acute improvements in both the accuracy of cervical joint position sense (CJPS) and pressure pain threshold. In contrast, the control group, which only observed a massage video, showed largely unchanged outcomes (Preiss, Beinert, et al., 2024). Despite initial evidence supporting the effectiveness of balance training and visuo-motor training for neck pain, several key research gaps remain. Previous studies have either investigated very short (acute) interventions or longer-term balance training programs; however, it remains unclear whether visuo-motor training conducted over several weeks produces sustainable effects—particularly in a real occupational context. Moreover, the combination of both training approaches has not yet been systematically investigated. Another important aspect concerns the populations and settings studied. It is currently unknown whether the positive effects of such interventions also translate to the everyday working environment of office workers with non-specific neck pain. Finally, follow-up studies are lacking to examine the persistence of the achieved effects after completion of the intervention.

Research questions:
1) How do visuo-motor head tracking, balance training, the combination of both approaches, and observation of a massage video differ with regard to pain intensity, functional disability, joint position sense, and pressure pain threshold in office workers with chronic non-specific neck pain immediately after a four-week intervention, and are these effects maintained at the eight-week follow-up?

2) Do the individual groups show changes over time (PRE, POST, FU) in the primary outcomes?

3) Do the groups differ in their change scores ΔPOST–PRE, ΔFU–POST, and ΔFU–PRE for the primary outcomes?

Methods:
The study is designed as a four-arm randomized controlled intervention trial. Office workers with chronic non-specific neck pain are included. Following baseline assessments, participants are randomly assigned to one of four groups:
(1) visuo-motor head tracking-Training,
(2) balance training,
(3) a combination of visuo-motor training and balance training (dual-task),
(4) an active control group (observation of a massage video).
The interventions last four weeks, with three sessions per week of approximately 17 minutes each, and are conducted in a workplace-based setting. Measurements are performed before the intervention (PRE), immediately after the intervention (POST), and eight weeks after completion of the intervention (follow-up).
Primary outcome measures include pain intensity (NRS), functional disability (NPAD-D), cervical joint position sense (CJPS), and pressure pain threshold (PPT). Statistical analysis is performed using mixed ANOVA to examine group and time effects.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Office and administrative employees who regularly work in front of a computer screen
Age between 18 and 65 years
Chronic non-specific neck pain lasting for at least three months
Non-specific neck pain occurring on the majority of days during the previous month (≥ 50% of days); participation is also possible if no acute pain is present on the day of the baseline assessment
Exclusion criteria:
Severe visual or hearing impairments
Serious medical conditions (e.g., type 2 diabetes mellitus, rheumatic diseases, neurological or vestibular disorders, or other chronic underlying diseases*)
Ankle sprain (inversion/supination injury) within the past three months
Radiculopathies (disorders or damage affecting nerve roots)
Previous surgery, fractures, spinal infections, or myelopathy of the cervical spine (spinal cord damage)
Acute injuries or instability of the ankle or knee joint
Severe balance disorders (e.g., due to neurological conditions or dizziness)
Severe osteoarthritis of the ankle or knee joint preventing participation in balance training
*Chronic underlying diseases refer to conditions that may have a significant impact on the participant’s general health status, such as multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, cancer, or epilepsy.
Failure to meet the minimum adherence requirement of completing at least 10 out of the 12 scheduled training sessions
